articles.title_orig: Nvidia CEO Faces Senate Scrutiny Over China Chip and Spy Scandal
articles.title_zh: Nvidia CEO Faces Senate Scrutiny Over China Chip and Spy Scandal
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of AI tech giant Nvidia effective immediately following a scandal involving an alleged spy, the company's board of directors announced Thursday.
The decision came amid an investigation into Huang's affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspect was spying for China. President Trump said this week the FBI is investigating romantic and business ties between Huang and suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. The two aren't related.
Nvidia's board had been preparing to oust Huang , two sources familiar with the matter confirmed to CBS News on Wednesday night, plans that were first reported by the Wall Street Journal.
Huang's departure also follows a New York Times report Wednesday that five employees at Nvidia came forward alleging Huang was romantically involved with a subordinate, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare.
The Times also reported Huang and Powell, who are both married to other people, were caught on video being affectionate at a conference in March, according to two Nvidia employees. The Times has not seen the video and CBS News has not verified the report.
After Huang's resignation was announced Thursday, the Reuters news agency reported that Huang also had an intimate relationship with a second employee, according to two people familiar with the matter. The agency only identified the employee as a woman.
The company's interim CEO will be Colette Kress, who is currently Nvidia's chief financial officer and will continue in that role.
"The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," Harvey Jones, who was announced as the company's first board chair, said in a statement.
Kress has been Nvidia's CFO since she joined the company in 2013. She previously worked in finance roles at tech companies like Cisco and Microsoft for nearly 25 years.
Nvidia was co-founded by Huang in 1993. It became one of the most valuable companies in the world by designing the powerful semiconductors that fuel many of the world's leading AI firms, making its technology highly sensitive and subject to export controls limiting sales to China.
Nvidia's stock plunged as news emerged of the company's turmoil, potentially erasing almost $500 billion in value. In Thursday's trading, the stock price closed down 4.3% at $166.19.
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was an executive at Megaspeed International , a Singapore-based data center company whose website touts its partnership with Nvidia.
Megaspeed grew with the help of access to Nvidia's restricted AI computer chips. According to U.S. investigators, Alice Huang was able to gain access to 240,000 chips that were banned from being exported to China. Megaspeed is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China.
In Washington, top Democrats on Capitol Hill have expressed concerns over whether Jensen Huang's ties to Alice Huang may have compromised U.S. national security.
Following Jensen Huang's resignation, Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts said his departure doesn't absolve him or the company from the scandal.
"Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Warren said in a statement.
Before Huang resigned, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News the departure could help China in the competition between Beijing and the U.S.
"With him out as CEO, China could significantly narrow the gap versus the U.S.," Ives said. He added: "The problem now is that there's no replacement for Jensen. It's a black eye moment for him, for Nvidia, and actually the U.S. tech industry. I'd say it's dark day for, you know, U.S. technology."
Following Thursday morning's announcement, Mr. Trump said on his Truth Social platform that there was "only one man" who could replace Huang: former Apple CEO Tim Cook .
Mr. Trump had a close relationship with Huang, who has attended AI-focused White House events and traveled with Mr. Trump to China. Late last year, Mr. Trump granted Nvidia the right to sell advanced H200 chips to "approved customers" in China, with the U.S. government getting a 25% cut — a major coup for Huang, who has long sought to sell more technology to the Chinese market. The deal did not cover Nvidia's even more advanced Blackwell and Rubin systems.
In a radio interview Thursday, Mr. Trump brought up that he gave Huang a National Medal of Science earlier this year. "What a horrible thing that is," he said of the situation involving Huang, adding, "That's so sad to see that happen."
In a statement accompanying her appointment as interim CEO, Kress said that the company's focus will be on "serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders."
"NVIDIA's strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years," Kress said.
The board said it will be conducting a search for a permanent CEO and will consider internal and external candidates.
Isabel  Vincent , Jennifer  Jacobs , Aimee  Picchi and Jo Ling  Kent contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s push to restore Nvidia CEO could haunt the company in Congress
articles.title_zh: Trump’s push to restore Nvidia CEO could haunt the company in Congress
articles.content_orig:
One of the most dramatic about-faces in corporate America's history, Jensen Huang's return to the helm of AI chipmaker Nvidia spurred an equally historic record in the options market. More than 11 million options contracts traded on Nvidia stock Monday, the most active single day of trading for the stock's options in history. That outpaces the 9 million options traded on the Invesco QQQ Trust , and compares to 14 million traded on the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY) . Despite Nvidia's monstrous 31% rally and options volume that was more than five times the 30-day average, positioning in the flows was not abnormally bullish. Of the top 10 trades by dollar amount, two big put sales stood out, but there were no likely outright call buys, based on data from Barchart and SpotGamma. If there was speculative call-buying, it was dwarfed by big trades between the 160 and 170 strikes, where four million options traded for almost $2 billion.
Nvidia closed near $165. "People are mostly just trying to collect a lot of premiums through short vol trades and rolls once they heard about Jensen Huang, take advantage of the vol drop more than anything else," Jason DeLorenzo, founder of Volland, an options-analytics software, said by phone. "It seems like options traders were all repricing, which created record volume, but did not create any obvious one-sidedness." Just under 6.7 million calls traded versus 4.3 million puts, according to Cboe LiveVol data. About 2.4 million calls were likely initiated by buyers, compared with 1.6 million purchasing puts, exchange data show. Open interest in calls was highest at the 170-strike, while open interest in puts was highest at the 150-strike, Barchart data show.

articles.title_zh: Nvidia live updates: Nvidia stock falls as exuberance fades after Jensen Huang's return as CEO
articles.content_orig:
The mood inside Nvidia was jubilant as CEO Jensen Huang walked in on Monday to chants of his first name and three floors of cheering employees, according to a video shared with CNBC.
"Thank you all for the second chances," Huang said to the crowd. "I'm going to be a better CEO the second time around."
Nvidia announced on Monday that Huang had been reinstated as CEO , effective immediately.
It was a dramatic turn in the chaos that's enveloped the chip giant and the entire tech trade since reports surfaced that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy . The reports sparked renewed investigations into the smuggling of restricted Nvidia chips into China.
Huang admitted to an affair in a note to employees on Nov. 8 and resigned as CEO on Nov. 12. The New York Times and Reuters subsequently reported that Huang had relationships with two employees, one of whom was a direct report.
On Monday, cupcakes were circulating at the office with "Jensen is back" written on them, according to a person inside the company who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
There was a sense of excitement among employees, as well as frustration over how the events of the last two weeks unfolded, the person said, adding that last Wednesday's all-hands meeting was a turning point.
A side-by-side photo was circulated internally of an all-hands meeting hosted by Huang, contrasted with the most recent meeting with a group of executives and board members sitting on stage, according to the person.
Now, all eyes are on the board, which said just last week that Huang would not be coming back .
"It's embarrassing for the board," said a former Nvidia employee who was at the company for more than 15 years, who asked not to be named in order to share insight into the company.
"It's likely that the board will change and some people may step down, some people may be replaced," the former employee said. They added that many employees "felt that the board acted too hastily."
President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he played a large role in Huang's return, and that he spoke to the board "directly and indirectly."
Trump called into the board meeting that was held on Sunday, CNBC confirmed.

articles.title_orig: CF40 Research: China’s real estate adjustment may be nearing its end—and its external surplus could stop widening
articles.title_zh: CF40 Research: China’s real estate adjustment may be nearing its end—and its external surplus could stop widening
articles.content_orig:
Late last month, CF40 Research , the research arm of the China Finance 40 Forum-a leading non-governmental think tank specializing in economics, shared its annual flagship report, China’s Economy: Toward a New Paradigm—Drivers, Trends, and Policy Implications , at its 2026 Bund Summit .
Guo Kai , President of CF40 Research and a former Chinese central bank official, kindly shared a copy and allowed me to share an excerpt.
The following passages are from the report’s English text. They have been rearranged and intervening material omitted; section headings and this introduction are mine. Corporate debt and profit figures below refer to its sample of A-share-listed companies outside finance and petroleum.
By 2026, the current real estate adjustment may not yet have fully run its course, but signs of structural stabilization have begun to emerge. After five years of deep adjustment, housing sales, investment, inventories, and developers’ balance sheets have entered a new phase, while house-price declines have begun to moderate. Few would expect the real estate sector to return to its former “golden age,” but the drag from the ongoing adjustment on the economy has diminished markedly at the margin. In other words, real estate is gradually shifting from the economy’s largest source of downward pressure toward a more stable influence.
Based on our analysis of international real estate corrections, China’s current real estate adjustment has already been considerable in both duration and magnitude, and the market has likely entered a bottoming phase. Further adjustment remains possible, but another sharp contraction appears unlikely.
Since the start of 2026, China’s real estate market has begun to show signs of “structural stabilization.” We selected 33 core cities for analysis, including the four first-tier cities—Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, and Shenzhen—and major second-tier cities such as Hangzhou, Suzhou, Qingdao, Wuhan, and Hefei. We find that house prices, the floor area of new homes sold, and existing-home transaction volumes have all shown signs of stabilizing in these cities. House prices have even risen modestly in a few core cities. By contrast, real estate markets in most third- and fourth-tier cities remain weak. In other words, stabilization is concentrated in core cities rather than broad-based, which is why we refer to it as “structural stabilization.”
Thus, for the 33 core cities, if new starts continue to decline sharply, excess housing inventory could be rapidly reduced, potentially giving way to a shortage. This would provide additional support for house prices and demand and could accelerate the housing market’s recovery.
Over the past few years, the deep adjustment in the real estate market has been the main driver of the widening current account surplus. The underlying mechanism is that the real estate downturn led to a sharp decline in the investment rate, while the saving rate adjusted with a lag. The resulting widening of the saving–investment gap translated directly into a larger current account surplus.
As the real estate market gradually stabilizes, the drag from real estate investment will diminish, while household precautionary saving will stop rising. The saving–investment gap will therefore narrow, and the current account surplus will stabilize at a high level rather than continue to widen. This process bears some resemblance to the decline in China’s current account surplus after 2008, when the RMB 4 trillion stimulus package drove a sharp expansion in domestic investment, significantly narrowing the saving–investment gap.
By contrast, the stabilization of the manufacturing capacity cycle since 2024 has clearly not relied on comparable demand-side stimulus. Instead, the sequence has been “supply adjustment first, followed by a moderate recovery in demand”: a market-driven process in which firms voluntarily slowed investment and retired inefficient capacity in response to weak demand. This differs fundamentally from the post-2016 cyclical reversal driven by a sharp rebound in demand.
According to CF40 research, the new economy’s total value added rose from about 6.1% of GDP in 2018 to 10.4% in 2025, while the corresponding share for real estate fell from 12.7% to 8.4%. By 2025, the new economy’s total value-added share had surpassed that of real estate and had become an important component of GDP.
A defining characteristic of new-economy firms is their greater emphasis on R&D and their ability to generate more operating revenue and profits with less debt. In 2025, new-economy firms accounted for only 11.9% of the total interest-bearing debt of firms in the full sample, compared with 17.8% of total operating revenue and 29.5% of total net profits across the sample. Their share of total R&D expenditure was even higher, at 47.6%. As the new economy accounts for a growing share of China’s economy, the country’s growth model will gradually evolve.
The negative wealth effect of the real estate adjustment is fading, but households’ propensity to consume remains well below its pre-pandemic level, while further improvements in social security and public services are constrained by fiscal pressures. Rather than rising sharply, the consumption rate is therefore more likely to stabilize as the drag from real estate fades. If supportive policies are fully implemented, the consumption rate could gradually rise.
Moreover, the more advanced a manufacturing industry, the lower the share of output going to compensation of employees tends to be. For example, compensation of employees accounts for only 7.8% and 7.6% of gross output in electrical machinery and equipment manufacturing and automobile manufacturing, respectively—two industries that together encompass the “new three.” The corresponding share is 8.7% in computer, communications, and other electronic equipment manufacturing, the industry most closely associated with AI.
On a value-added basis, compensation of employees accounts for 36%, 42%, and 47% in these three industries, respectively, all below the service-sector average. This means that even if the new economy continues to expand rapidly and drive economic growth, households’ share of income in primary distribution will not automatically increase and could even decline. This is because these new-economy industries allocate a smaller share of their output to compensation of employees than the current economy-wide average.
On monetary policy, emphasis should move further away from pursuing credit-volume expansion toward lowering interest rates, improving inflation expectations, and restoring nominal demand. Real estate no longer performs its previous role in credit expansion, while the new economy is relatively less dependent on bank credit. Growth in bank lending and total social financing is therefore increasingly difficult to use on its own as a measure of whether monetary policy is sufficiently accommodative.
One possible aggregate benchmark is that “nominal growth in broad fiscal expenditure should exceed nominal GDP growth.” At present, local governments face multiple constraints, including declining land-related revenues, debt resolution efforts, and rising mandatory spending commitments. Near-term fiscal expansion will therefore need to rely more heavily on the central government.
The new economy has demonstrated China’s capacity to create new productive capacity, but the more important issue for the next stage is how to translate that capacity into household income and final consumption. New-economy firms have high R&D spending, high productivity, and low reliance on debt—an important direction for economic transformation. However, if the industrial structure merely shifts from traditional manufacturing toward more advanced manufacturing, higher productivity will not necessarily translate automatically into a larger household income share or a higher consumption rate.

articles.title_orig: Government launches inquiry into Birmingham housing scheme 'exploitation'
articles.title_zh: Government launches inquiry into Birmingham housing scheme 'exploitation'
articles.content_orig:
The government has announced an independent inquiry into allegations rogue landlords in Birmingham are making huge profits by exploiting a housing scheme.
BBC Panorama reported last month that some companies in the city were taking advantage of the Supported Exempt Accommodation (SEA) system, intended to provide housing along with care and support for vulnerable people.
There have been claims of fraud, crime, poor housing and firms receiving housing benefits on behalf of residents but not giving them the support they are meant to.
A government spokesperson said an eight-week investigation would begin immediately, with initial findings and recommendations reported to ministers in the new year.
Sir David Pearson, chair of the Supported Housing Advisory Panel and social care expert, has been appointed to lead the investigation.
The government added the investigation would examine the scale of the problems in the city's SEA sector, including the quality of accommodation and support, use of public money, and effectiveness of oversight and regulation.
In a letter confirming the appointment, housing secretary Angela Rayner asked Pearson to lead a "rapid independent investigation" into the claims.
She said the investigation should focus on Birmingham, given consistent reports that the area was at the "epicentre of concerns" about poor-quality supported accommodation, while considering the extent to which any findings can be applied to the rest of the country.
"Good-quality supported housing can turn lives around and provide people with the support they need to live as independently as possible," Rayner wrote.
"There are increasing reports, however, that this system is being abused, with vulnerable people exploited at the expense of the taxpayer."
SEA is designed for people in the UK with additional needs, including people recovering from addiction and women fleeing domestic abuse.
In many cases it works well for people, but BBC investigations over the past five years have uncovered stories of vulnerable people, including care leavers and people with mental health problems, being let down by the system designed to support them .
Some residents said they had been left living alongside drug dealers and criminals, and fearing for their lives, despite some providers reportedly claiming more than £200 a week at the time for every person they house.
Supported housing expenditure had risen faster in Birmingham than the national average in recent years, a government spokesperson said.
Pat McFadden, Work and Pensions Secretary, said there were "real concerns" about how the system was operating.
"Sir David's investigation will get to the bottom of what's going on, and where we find wrongdoing, we will act to make sure money is spent on supporting people who need it," he said.
The council paid out £404.4m for SEA in the 2024-25 financial year, with a further £211.8m paid between April and July 2026.
More than 34,000 people in the city currently live in SEA, compared to about 22,000 living in London, despite its population being more than seven times larger.
The BBC has previously heard evidence of claims that some housing providers were willing to make benefit claims for people who did not live in their properties .
Preet Gill, the Labour MP for Birmingham Edgbaston, said she welcomed the independent review.
"I have campaigned on exempt accommodation for nearly a decade and worked with residents, the council and police to shut down Saif Lodge, the first exempt accommodation property in the country to be closed in 2021," she said.
"Neighbours have had enough of the antisocial behaviour, and vulnerable people are being let down while some providers profit."
It is not the first time politicians have investigated the issue.
An inquiry by the Levelling Up, Housing and Communities Committee in 2022 reported that some vulnerable people had faced rape and exploitation by landlord "gangsters" in England's "complete mess" of an exempt housing system.
That was two years after Birmingham was named as one of five pilot projects designed to improve quality, enforcement, oversight and value for money in the sector.
Tuesday's announcement follows a recent letter to the prime minister from councillors Robert Alden and Ken Wood, demanding urgent intervention.
Campaigners have called for action for years, under both Conservative and Labour governments.
Alden, the councillor for Erdington and leader of the Birmingham Conservative group, said it was right that the government examines "why Birmingham has become the epicentre of this crisis and what must change".
"Residents deserve answers about how this was allowed to happen.
"Vulnerable people placed in badly run accommodation deserve proper support, and neighbourhoods suffering the consequences deserve action."
Charities, residents and politicians told Panorama last month that parts of the system were being exploited.
The programme found property agents drawing people into the taxpayer-funded system using social media videos offering free rooms, PlayStation consoles and holidays.
Patricia Coleman-Taylor, who runs Birmingham anti-poverty charity Narthex, said many vulnerable people were being used as "cash cows to generate income" that goes from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) into "the back pocket of the landlords".
Alysha told Panorama that she had moved into SEA 18 months ago, a survivor of domestic abuse.
She had nowhere to go and no family living nearby, so she was made homeless and relying on universal credit.
"I never thought I'd be homeless and I never thought my marriage would break down, but it did," she said.
"I felt extremely alone. I needed help getting myself back on to my feet, and that's how I got myself into supported accommodation."
She has since lived in three different SEA properties but admitted her experience was far from the fresh start she needed.
Alysha was forced to leave her first placement after just six months.
"There was one day at about 05:30 in the morning, where I was woken up to screaming and growling and banging.
"They'd been fighting really badly. The house was covered in blood, police were called, and the house was no longer safe."
Her second SEA initially looked "amazing" with brand new kitchen appliances and mattresses but Alysha quickly learnt it was not as it appeared.
Managed by a private provider, Alysha said she was promised weekly counselling sessions, access to food banks, and help with GPs.
"But it's not the case, it's not the case at all," she said.
"They're not interested, they come and they just want you to sign that paper to say Alysha's done support this week and that's it."
She added that the home had been left without heating at one point in the winter.
Jane and Melvin, residents living in Selly Oak, said the house next door to them was converted into SEA.
The couple admit at times they felt unsafe in their own home with the tenants of the property having involvement with guns, knives, and drugs.
"There were people overdosing," Jane recalled, adding: "Twice the front door was kicked in by people who didn't live there."
Melvin said: "Ambulances would pull up with their blue lights flashing at two or three o'clock of a morning.
"There were people running up and down screaming, fights going on... there was one episode where one afternoon the chap was being chased by someone with a knife.
"If he hadn't have been athletic, he'd have been killed."
Jane said she and her husband never objected to the property being used to support people in need.
But she felt as though those living in the SEA were left to run "amuck".
"I think they were lacking the support that they needed, really," she explained.

articles.title_orig: China Probes Fourth Politburo Member in Major Leadership Shakeup
articles.title_zh: China Probes Fourth Politburo Member in Major Leadership Shakeup
articles.content_orig:
The Communist Party chief of Shanghai, considered one of the potential heirs to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, has suddenly been placed under investigation –– marking an escalation of an anti-corruption purge that’s already ensnared a large swath of the country’s top talent .
Chen Jining, 62, who has run China’s largest city and financial center since October 2022, is facing a corruption charge and is suspected of “serious violations of discipline,” state media Xinhua said on Tuesday evening.
It is a stunning downfall for Chen, who was seen as a rising political star and even being mentioned among potential successors to longtime leader Xi by China watchers.
Xi, who is all but certain to assume a precedent-breaking fourth term in office next year, has executed an unrelenting anti-corruption drive for well over a decade that has brought down senior political, military and judiciary figures once thought untouchable. The speed and scale that effort has reached unseen levels in recent months.
Chen becomes the fourth of the 24 member politburo –– the top-echelon of power in China –– to fall since the last party congress in 2022.
The investigation is being conducted by China’s main anti-corruption body, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection.
Chen’s last public appearance appears to be Thursday, November 19, when he inspected the headquarters of a Chinese shipping conglomerate.
Unsurprisingly, government platforms in Shanghai have quickly taken down posts mentioning Chen.
Trained as an environmental scientist, the urbane and English-speaking Chen rose through the party ranks in the past two decades. Before moving to Shanghai, he was mayor of Beijing and orchestrated the 2022 Winter Olympics Games in the capital.
His appointment to the top party job in Shanghai marked a quick elevation. The post usually paves the way for further promotion to the Politburo Standing Committee - the pinnacle of the party’s power structure. Both Xi and China’s former leader Jiang Zemin have followed this path.
It can be lonely at the top. And that’s just how China’s leader likes it
Prior to his Beijing mayorship, Chen spent over a decade at the Ministry of Environment and Ecology. He also served as the president of the Tsinghua University in Beijing, one of China’s most prestigious academic institutions.
After earning a master’s degree in civil and environmental engineering from Tsinghua in 1980s, Chen went to study at London’s Imperial College, where he earned a doctorate degree.
Just in the past two month, Xi’s clampdown of top officials saw the downfall of Beijing’s deputy mayor and a retired former mayor of Chongqing who had withstood several prior political storms.
The party’s top military decision-making body, the usually seven-member Central Military Commission, is now down to only two members with one of those being Xi himself .
Since Xi, 73, came to power over 14 years ago millions of rank-and-file officials have also been  caught in his dragnet.
Between 2012 and 2022, over 500 ministerial-level officials were convicted, removed from their posts, and expelled from the party for corruption, according to official data from the party’s Central Commission of Discipline Inspection (CCDI) – with more than 410 officials purged in the last three years alone.

articles.title_orig: US lawmakers vow to investigate Jensen Huang and Trump over Nvidia scandal
articles.title_zh: US lawmakers vow to investigate Jensen Huang and Trump over Nvidia scandal
articles.content_orig:
Republican pushback to Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO is growing, despite President Donald Trump earlier downplaying any blowback from his party.
The chairs of the GOP-led House intelligence and foreign affairs committees as well as the House select committee on the Chinese Communist Party criticized Nvidia in a joint statement on Monday. Reps. Rick Crawford, Brian Mast and John Moolenaar said the company’s “brief internal investigation” and reinstatement of Huang “do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed.”
GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan of North Carolina also blasted Huang’s reinstatement as a “mistake.”
“Today, we sent a signal that one man’s financial impact on our economy outweighs the importance of good governance, good citizenship, and adherence to the law,” the North Carolina Republican wrote in a post on X . “That is a dangerous precedent to set, and one I believe will come at a significant cost to our country in the long run.”
GOP Sen. Kevin Cramer of North Dakota wrote , “The legal and reputational risk of hiring a CEO who may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws is now born by the board of Nvidia, but the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens.”
Sen. John Curtis of Utah went as far as to scrutinize the input Nvidia said it received from “senior levels of the United States government” that Huang poses no national security risk.
“Nvidia’s board says it relied on input from senior U.S. officials to conclude that bringing Jensen Huang back posed no national security risk. I have some questions. Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?” Curtis said .
Arkansas GOP Sen. Tom Cotton, who is known as a China hawk, said in a post on X that Congress must investigate further and called for his chip export bill to pass.
“The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it’s not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back,” said Cotton, who is the outgoing Senate Intelligence Committee chairman. “Congress has much to investigate and we will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip export-control bills, including my Chip Security Act, one way or the other.”
That legislation proposes requiring some kind of “location verification mechanism” on advanced chips and directs the Commerce Department to study “other potential chip security mechanisms.”
Attorney General Todd Blanche on Monday evening, however, refused to answer during an interview with Fox News whether Huang had been cleared of any national security concerns or potential legal violations before being reinstated.
CNN reported earlier Monday that several other Republicans have criticized or questioned the move to reinstate Huang — including Sens. John Cornyn and Pete Ricketts and Rep. Don Bacon.
Earlier Monday in an interview with CNBC, Trump dismissed any concerns from GOP lawmakers saying, “When I speak to them, they’re going to be great.”
This story has been updated with additional information.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine insists attack on Russian ships in Libya was self-defence
articles.title_zh: Ukraine insists attack on Russian ships in Libya was self-defence
articles.content_orig:
Vantor satellite image shows a vessel partly visible in the water beside a pier in Benghazi. Scattered debris and darkened areas are visible along the pier on Nov. 22, 2026.
Ukraine sank a Russian warship moored at a port in Libya using naval drones, said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky .
Forces deployed seven Ukrainian-made drones that struck and sank the Russian corvette Mercury, which was carrying a combat helicopter, Zelensky said Monday. A second ship, the Russian container carrier MV ANGARA, which Zelensky said was being used to “transport weapons,” was also hit.
Footage released by Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense appeared to show sea drones speeding toward the warship—one of the newest in Russia's fleet—before it erupted into a giant ball of flames.
The Mercury was commissioned a year after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and incorporates some of Moscow’s latest shipbuilding technology, Russian state news agency TASS reported when the ship joined the fleet in May 2023.
Russia’s Defense Ministry has yet to comment on the attack.
Zelensky hailed the sinking of the warship as an example of an “exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war.”
Late Monday morning, Zelensky made a virtual appearance at the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin, where peace opportunities for Ukraine and suspected Russian violations of NATO airspace were top of the agenda.
“Today, Russia can feel our response all the way from western Siberia, where its oil refineries are burning, to the coast of Libya, where its warships are sinking,” Zelensky said as he addressed attendees. “We have offered Russia steps to reduce the fighting dozens, dozens of times, and we have never been the ones to raise the stakes. But, unfortunately, Russia gives us no peaceful response.”
The strikes against the corvette, conducted around 2,400 kilometers (1,500 miles) from the front line in Ukraine, underscore Kyiv's long-range strike capabilities.
The Mercury had been in the port of Benghazi to refuel under a maritime cooperation agreement before its planned return to Russia, according to Libya’s Government of National Stability (GNS). In the wake of the strikes, the GNS, which controls eastern Libya and has a longstanding military relationship with Russia, said it had filed an official complaint with the U.N. Secretary-General and Security Council over threats to maritime security, arguing that the country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war.
The U.N. Support Mission in Libya called for an “immediate, independent, and transparent investigation,” offered U.N. assistance, and warned against drawing Libya into a wider confrontation.
The Foreign Ministry of the internationally-recognized northwestern Libyan government expressed "grave concern" over the attack, insisting that “the continuation of the war between ‌Russia and Ukraine gives neither side the right to conduct military operations on ⁠Libyan territory or ​in its territorial ​waters.”
U.S.-mediated talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations resumed earlier this month after a nine-month hiatus, but there is still no clear pathway to peace.
President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Chinese President Xi Jinping met for a historic sit-down at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit last week. Trump and Putin had a one-on-one conversation on the sidelines beforehand, but all communications failed to produce any meaningful progress toward ending the Russia-Ukraine war.
The strike in Libya followed a separate drone attack on a Russian cargo vessel in the eastern Gulf of Finland on Saturday, according to Finland's Ministry of Defense.
The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad when it was struck Saturday morning.
The vessel caught fire and drifted into Finnish territorial waters before being towed out Sunday by a Russian rescue vessel, following a Finnish-led response involving Estonia and Russia.
While Kyiv has not claimed responsibility for the attack, Aki-Mauri Huhtinen, director of communications for the Finnish Defense Forces, told local media “it is likely that Ukraine” was behind the strike.
TIME has reached out to Ukraine's Defense Ministry for comment.
The Kremlin described the attack on the Russia bulk carrier as escalating tensions in international waters. "All coastal countries are certainly concerned about this. This is very dangerous. It is escalating tensions in the region,” said Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, according to TASS .
The U.S. Treasury previously sanctioned the Sparta II in 2022, alleging that the vessel was linked to Russian military logistics company Oboronlogistika.
NATO chief Mark Rutte pledged Saturday that the alliance would “defend every inch of Polish territory,” speaking to reporters in Warsaw a day after two Russian missiles and a drone crashed in Polish territory.
Two missiles fell in Polish territory , with one landing near the town of Nowy Lipowiec, in the eastern part of the country, while another missile was discovered in a forest in southeastern Polish territory. Remnants of a drone were also found scattered across the southeastern part of the country.
Polish prosecutors said that all three fell in undeveloped areas with no injuries or significant property damage reported. All three areas remain under surveillance.
"I don't want to leave any room for interpretation—we know for sure that what fell on Polish soil came from Russia," Prime Minister Donald Tusk claimed during a press conference. “While there were no casualties or damage, it clearly demonstrates the scale of Russia's attack on Ukraine and the fact that the coming months will be filled with significant challenges.”
Russia has not claimed responsibility for the projectiles.
A meeting of NATO's North Atlantic Council took place Monday to discuss the violation of Poland’s airspace.
"It is ⁠clear that this ​is ⁠a dangerous incident. ‌It comes from Russia," Rutte said in Berlin. "Whether it is ⁠intentional or not has to be decided, of course, by authorities. I will never speculate."
Rutte also struck a defiant tone during a press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, during which he said that “for every incident in Europe, more support for Ukraine, not less support” will be provided.
The European Union on Monday presented a sweeping new sanctions package in a bid to increase economic pressure on Moscow to end the war.
The package is set to expand restrictions to a further 60 Russian banks, alongside cryptocurrency and payment platforms. It will also target Russia's energy sector by prohibiting European companies from helping build, operate, or repair Russian energy infrastructure, while restricting Europeans from serving on the governing bodies of companies in Russia.
“The aim is to keep pressure on Russia to end their war of aggression in Ukraine. And we will continue to propose new sanctions until Russia shows genuine intent for a lasting peace in Ukraine,” said European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen.
The proposed measures also seek to further isolate Moscow by restricting visas for former Russian combatants and banning Russian teams and athletes from competing under the country's flag for any sporting events in the E.U.
The European Commission added that it was seeking tighter restrictions on tourist visas, alongside additional measures affecting individual artists.
Kaja Kallas, the E.U.’s foreign policy chief, hailed the package and said any such “diplomacy to end Russia’s war needs to be backed up by pressure on the aggressor.”
The new set of sanctions will need to be agreed and approved by the 27-member states unanimously before they can come into force.

articles.title_orig: Russian governor detained in rare criminal case against regional leader
articles.title_zh: Russian governor detained in rare criminal case against regional leader
articles.content_orig:
The governor of Russia's northern Murmansk region has been arrested on corruption charges in the first detention of a regional leader for five years.
Andrei Chibis, 47, is suspected of embezzlement and misappropriation of  more than a billion roubles ($12.2.m; £9.3m) set aside to build an Arctic highway, as well as a further 39m roubles from the Murmansk construction budget.
Chibis is reported to have been detained as he arrived on a visit to Moscow on Monday and was taken in for questioning.
He denies wrongdoing but has made no public comment. His wife Yevgenia Chibis said "anyone who knows our family understands how ridiculous this is".
In a post on social media, she said her husband sincerely believed in the Murmansk region and thanked people for their words of support: "We really need them right now."
Chibis worked for several years as deputy minister for construction and housing, before becoming governor of Murmansk in 2019.
Murmansk is a key military point for Russia in the Arctic and is home to the Russian navy's Northern fleet.
Chibis was re-elected two years ago after surviving a knife attack and is considered an active supporter of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Governors are seen as representing the Kremlin, and Vladimir Putin removed several in the months after the war began in February 2022.
However, until now no regional governor has been arrested since the start of the war, even though plenty of high-ranking officials have been detained in that time.
The Murmansk governor is one of a number of officials suspected of corruption by the Russian interior ministry's investigative department which, according to reports, alleged that a criminal group was set up in 2022 to embezzle money from the regional budget and move it abroad, including to Kyrgyzstan.
Another part of the case involves alleged fraud surrounding the rebuilding of a motorway between the two Arctic towns of Apatity and Kirovsk, which are 15km (9.3 miles) apart.
According to Russian news agency Interfax, a court will decide whether Chibis will remain in custody at a hearing on Wednesday.
He has been sanctioned by both the UK and EU, which accuses him of involvement in the illegal transportation of Ukrainian children to Russia and their adoption by Russian families.

articles.title_orig: Russia accuses NATO member Estonia of hostile actions ‘on the verge of unleashing open war’
articles.title_zh: Russia accuses NATO member Estonia of hostile actions ‘on the verge of unleashing open war’
articles.content_orig:
Russia's Foreign Ministry has lashed out at Estonia's government, accusing the NATO member of carrying out a range of "hostile actions" and putting the Baltic state "on the verge of unleashing open war" with Moscow.
The outburst underscores rising tensions between Russia and countries on NATO's eastern flank and comes after Estonia announced it will close its road border crossings with Russia from Dec. 1.
Russia's ministry said Monday it had lodged a formal protest to Estonia's chargé d'affaires, Marek Uhtegi, over Tallinn's decision to close its border crossings and accused the European Union member of imposing a naval blockade against Moscow.
"The Estonian diplomat was again informed that such provocative and extremely dangerous actions are on the verge of unleashing open war with Russia," the ministry said in a statement, describing measures taken by Estonian lawmakers as "Russophobic."
The ministry also accused Estonia of "tacitly" providing its airspace for Ukrainian drone flights and sharply criticized Tallinn's ban on the transit of Russian and Belarusian grain through Estonian territory, referring to a policy that was introduced at the start of October.
Estonia, which shares a 294-kilometer (183-mile) border with Russia, swiftly denied ever allowing its territory to be used for military operations by another country.
It also responded to Russia's allegations by saying the Kremlin appears to be seeking to divert attention from its own efforts to undermine European security.
"Russian missiles have reached Polish territory, Danish security services have identified an assassination plot in Denmark orchestrated by Russian intelligence services, merchant vessels in the Black Sea are under constant threat from Russian attacks, and in Estonia, an arson attack targeting a defence industry company, planned on the orders of Russian military intelligence, was foiled," Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said Monday.
"All this is happening while Russia continues its war of aggression against Ukraine," he added.
The rhetoric marks a significant escalation in tensions between Estonia and Russia. Tallinn, a staunch Ukraine ally, has frequently raised the alarm over sabotage attacks against NATO countries that have been supporting Kyiv since Russia launched the full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022.
Earlier this month, Estonia said it would close road border crossings with Russia from Dec. 1 as it blames Moscow for an attempted "sabotage" of one of its defense companies, an allegation the Kremlin denies.
Tallinn has said the border closure will help to reduce Moscow's ability to conduct hostile activities against it and mitigate risks related to sanctions circumvention.
Ukraine has stepped up its attacks on Russian critical targets in recent weeks, damaging Russian President Vladimir Putin 's prized Crimea bridge , striking a Russian cargo ship in the Baltic Sea and destroying one of Russia's newest ships at a Libyan port .
The suspected Ukrainian attack on a Russian military-linked cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday prompted Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to warn that the Ukraine war is "spilling over" into its immediate vicinity.
Finland, one of NATO's newest members , has also closed its land border crossings with Russia.
Ukraine's latest attacks on some of Russia's most protected targets have demonstrated Kyiv's capabilities to hurt Moscow even without ample U.S. military support, according to Mario Bikarski, senior Europe and Central Asia analyst for Verisk Maplecroft, a political risk consultancy.
"Ukraine will continue to look for ways to degrade not only Russia's economy, but also its geostrategic interests in the wider region, including the Mediterranean and the Middle East," Bikarski said.
The prospect of an imminent peace deal between Russia and Ukraine appears to be slim, Bikarski said, although "the latest surge in diplomatic activity and mounting losses for both sides signals an appetite from all sides to reach an agreement."

articles.title_orig: One terminal command gave my forgotten Android device a desk job
articles.title_zh: One terminal command gave my forgotten Android device a desk job
articles.content_orig:
My kitchen junk drawer used to hold takeout menus and coupons, but it has since become a storage spot for old tablets or phones. Like me, you probably have a few devices lying around that are perfectly functional but don’t meet your daily driving needs. It’s tucked out of view, living out its life in a drawer until being erased and donated after someone asks why you’re holding onto outdated, unused devices. Thankfully, PhoneBox has a solution. You weren’t hoarding old tech; you were waiting for the proper use.
I had an old AllDoCube iPlay 50 mini Pro 8.4-inch tablet that seemed like the perfect candidate. I bought the tablet second-hand as a possible big-screen gaming and emulation tablet to use with a telescopic control deck, but I quickly found I vastly preferred just using a dedicated device. Since that realization, this decent little unit has lived its life in “the drawer.”
Getting PhoneBox up and running on my tablet and PC couldn’t have been simpler. After making sure that the Android tablet was in developer mode, the process was as easy as plugging the tablet in to my PC via USB and executing a single copied command in my Linux terminal. The script downloaded the PhoneBox 0.9.29 software for my PC, verified the downloaded checksum against the release, and walked me through a few quick Y/N installation questions. The script offers to create a systemd user service, so the desktop agent launches after initial login, and even asks if you’d like it to install the PhoneBox APK to your connected Android device.
I already had developer mode initialized on the tablet but had to go back and allow ADB over USB in settings. The total installation time from copying the script from the project website to everything running on my PC and tablet was less than a minute. The app is MIT-licensed , works on Android 5.0 or later, and requires sideloading, since it is not available on the Google Play Store .
Credit:
                                      Nick Indge Credit:

          
          Nick Indge
The installation script also prints its own uninstall script before it finishes. So often these days, getting rid of an unwanted app feels more difficult than installing it, so I appreciate the straightforward approach the developer has implemented.
The first time you fire up PhoneBox, you get live performance and diagnostic information from your PC, along with several pages of optional content that can be tweaked for your local setup to display information that’s pertinent to your uses.
Where PhoneBox really starts to shine is the widget catalog—a collection of free add-ons that can be added as pages to the tablet’s cycling page layouts. There are more general widgets, such as RSS feeds that display news highlights from your chosen sources, or simple displays like timers or world clocks.
I opted for a few different widgets that caught my eye. One let me view my library of installed Steam titles and launch them on my PC with a simple tap of the tablet screen. Another allows me to control smart home entities hosted by my Home Assistant server. I was controlling the lights in my office from my tablet within seconds of adding the widget. It’s brilliant.
Setting up additional widgets is as simple as adding them to the page layout from the PC’s web interface and hitting save. As soon as I updated things from the PC, the connected tablet immediately began reflecting the changes. I haven’t had the chance to test most of the 131 current options in the widget catalog, but the ones I did try were simple to modify and worked on the first try.
While I didn’t have any major issues with PhoneBox, I did notice a couple of early annoyances along the way. Windows users should be aware that the PC companion app on that OS is currently unsigned, and they should expect a SmartScreen notification when attempting to install the software.
All control settings live in the web interface rather than the phone or tablet you’re connecting. When I first started messing with PhoneBox, I noticed it displayed my weather location as Tallinn. Nothing against the capital of Estonia, but that’s not weather information that does me much good here in the US Midwest. When I went into the widget settings to change the report location, there was nothing to be found. It turns out that you have to change those settings from the general user preferences section rather than within the widget itself. Not a deal-breaker by any means, but a slight hiccup for someone who was new to the software.
Connecting the Android tablet with my PC over USB was totally painless, but I never got the wireless route to work in my testing. Users are meant to generate a QR code from the PhoneBox web interface on their PC and connect it to their device by scanning the code with their phone/tablet. Every time I tried to scan the code from my device’s camera app, the tablet refused. There’s no QR scanner built into the PhoneBox app, so if your camera app won’t cooperate, the documented path dead-ends. USB was my intended route anyway and works great, but if you’re planning a wireless-only setup, be prepared for possible friction. The documented flow needs your device camera to open the pairing link, and mine wasn’t in the mood.
These minor gripes should be smoothed over before the release of 1.0. The project is early, but it seems to be moving quickly. I tested and installed PhoneBox version 0.9.29, which was one of several releases pushed to the project’s GitHub in as many days. One item of history worth noting: On November 20, the project published a high-severity security advisory covering versions 0.9.23 and earlier. The vulnerability potentially allowed another app running on the connected Android device to execute commands or receive stored credentials from the host PC. The flaw no longer existed by the time I tested the package in version 0.9.29, but it’s a good reminder that you’re installing something with deep system access and should exercise appropriate caution.
As long as you’re part of the group that has an old phone or tablet lying around somewhere, and these days I expect that most of us are, then it’s an emphatic yes. Repurposing old devices to find new lives is one of the things that keeps me a tech hobbyist. I love finding genuinely useful and practical applications for devices that have been pushed aside by their manufacturers in favor of the latest and greatest in the lineup.
PhoneBox took a tablet that was forgotten in a junk drawer and destined for donation and gave it a new lease on life. I haven’t spent a single penny, but I now have a useful secondary display on my desk. The tablet is powered via a dedicated USB port on my PC, and only goes to sleep when my main monitor displays do. Go dig through those mystery drawers in your house, because this one is worthwhile.

articles.title_orig: Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza
articles.title_zh: Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza
articles.content_orig:
At least seven Palestinians, including a senior Hamas security official, have been killed in Israeli air strikes in the Gaza Strip, health officials and first responders say.
Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service, was targeted in western Gaza City, Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry said. The 50-year-old had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid by Israeli special forces .
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz announced that Abu Nahel was "eliminated" by the Israeli military.
The six other people were killed in two earlier air strikes elsewhere in Gaza.
Three people, including a teenage boy, were killed in the Wadi Gaza area, south of Gaza City, according to the health officials and first responders. The other three were killed at a police station in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis, they added.
Gaza's police force, which operates under the interior ministry, said two of its officers were among those who died in the second attack. It also accused Israel of "an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos" in the territory.
The Israeli military said it struck "military operatives" in both areas.
Witnesses said an Israeli drone targeted Naeem Abu Nahel as he was walking on a side street near a tent camp for displaced people in Gaza City.
Several other people were reportedly seriously injured in the strike.
The Israeli military said Abu Nahel had "possessed extensive institutional knowledge" about Hamas's internal security service - which is responsible for enforcing discipline, protecting infrastructure and rooting out informants - and that his death constituted "a blow to the apparatus's management capabilities".
It also alleged that he had advanced attacks on Israeli troops and civilians during the war and that it killed him "to remove the threat he posed".
Gaza's interior ministry said Abu Nahel's killing followed what it described as the internal security service's "important achievements in combating gangs collaborating with the occupation [Israel] and operating in areas under the control of its military".
Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.
The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to thousands of shelters for displaced families.
The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.
On Tuesday, the health ministry warned that there had been a rapid rise in cases of meningitis, with 272 reported in October - about eight times the usual monthly average.
Fifteen deaths had been attributed to the infection so far this year, including five reported between August and October, it said.
Israeli military body Cogat said on Monday it was "working to provide a dedicated humanitarian response" and that a newly approved package of pumps, generators, water tankers and medical equipment had been presented at a meeting with UN agencies.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,740 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title_orig: Denmark: Supreme Court backs hardline immigration law against 'non-Westerners'
articles.title_zh: Denmark: Supreme Court backs hardline immigration law against 'non-Westerners'
articles.content_orig:
Denmark's Supreme Court on Monday ruled in favor of a housing association that terminated 91 leases in order to prevent the label "hard ghetto" being applied to their housing complex. The decision align's with Copenhagen's hardline approach to immigration .
The court on Monday upheld Denmark 's 2018 "ghetto law," which allows for the relocation of "non-Western" residents from minority-heavy neighborhoods in order to foster integration . The Danish court ruling diverges from a top EU court decision last year that found application of the law could amount to discrimination.
The Danish laws requires social housing estates to rebuild, renovate and adjust their social mix if these become minority heavy, stipulating that 60% of apartments be rented to "Westerners" at market value by 2030.

Denmark's pioneering role in spearheading tougher immigration rules has made it a model for some in the EU . Denmark was also one of five countries that last week announced its intent to set up an asylum seeker deportation hub in Rwanda.
Danish Housing Minister Jacob Mark welcomed Monday's decision, saying it "strengthens security, social cohesion and integration."
The court's decision upheld a 2022 lower court ruling against seven tenants who fought their evictions in Nojsomhed, Helsingor, just north of Copenhagen.
In Monday's ruling, the law was found to be non-discriminatory when it comes to the eviction of "immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries" as it is not broadly based on ethnicity. The EU ruling focused on this particular aspect, saying the law would be discriminatory if criteria were race based, while ultimately allowing national courts to have the last say in the matter.
"The Supreme Court notes that applying the criterion of the law involves dividing people into two groups [immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries, and all other persons]. Both groups include a very large majority of different ethnic origins, and there will simultaneously be persons with the same ethnic origin in both groups," read the Danish court's ruling.

Tenants' associations estimate that 11,000 people across Denmark will have to be relocated to comply with the law.
The housing association in question issued a written statement saying that it was aware that the evictions would impact those affected, adding that it undertook measures to insure that residents found new homes.
According to Statistics Denmark's definition, "non-Western" countries include every country other than the 27 member states of the European Union, as well as Andorra, Australia, Britain, Canada, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, New Zealand, Northern Ireland, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, the United States and the Vatican.

articles.title_orig: Best Buy reports comparable sales growth of 6.1%, highest in five years
articles.title_zh: Best Buy reports comparable sales growth of 6.1%, highest in five years
articles.content_orig:
Best Buy on Tuesday beat Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines for its third fiscal quarter and raised its full-year guidance.
The consumer electronics retailer reported comparable sales growth of 6.1%, a significant beat over expectations of 2.3%, according to market intelligence platform StreetAccount. The company said that growth was its highest in five years. It reported a domestic comparable sales increase of 6.2% and international comparable sales growth of 4.9%.
"We have a tremendous amount of momentum," CEO Jason Bonfig told CNBC. "The fact that we saw pretty much broad-based growth across almost all of our categories is a lot of momentum that we're very excited about."
Best Buy also raised its guidance for the rest of the year. It's now expecting full-year revenue of between $43 billion and $43.3 billion compared with a previous expectation of between $42.3 billion and $42.8 billion. It's expecting comparable sales to be up 3.4% to 4% compared with prior guidance of between 1.9% and 3%.
The earnings report is the company's first since Bonfig took over as CEO from Corie Barry at the beginning of the month.
Bonfig said the retailer saw overperformance in both computing and gaming for the quarter, driven by recent game launches and a targeted product assortment.
Looking ahead into the holiday season, he said the Best Buy consumer remains "resilient," but that they are focused on getting value wherever they can.
"We did see not only our current customers continue to be engaged, but we actually did see more new customers come into the brand, as well as we had some customers that we re-engaged as well," Bonfig said. "So those are really, really positive signs for us in Q3, and all of that was factored into the way that we guided for Q4 and the rest of the year."
Here's how the company performed in the period ended Oct. 31 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
Best Buy reported net income of $353 million, or $1.66 per share, compared with $140 million, or 66 cents per share, the year prior. Adjusting for one-time items, including restructuring charges, Best Buy posted adjusted earnings of $1.62 per share.
Revenue rose to $10.24 billion from $9.67 billion in the year-ago period. Best Buy reported domestic revenue of $9.42 billion and international revenue of $820 million.
Tuesday's earnings are the latest in a series of strong reports from the retailer, which has been instituting a turnaround strategy to return to growth after getting hit by declining foot traffic, lower consumer sentiment, tariffs and memory costs .
Shares of Best Buy are up nearly 45% this year.
Bonfig told CNBC last quarter that the launch of " Grand Theft Auto VI " in the current quarter is expected to drive sales in the gaming category, which has been seeing gains over the past year. Last month, Best Buy launched a new gaming experience for customers featuring gaming content, technology and special offers, among other features.
"I think there'll still be opportunities for gaming to continue to drive our business moving forward," Bonfig told CNBC on Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: Some U.S. food banks see demand top pandemic levels
articles.title_zh: Some U.S. food banks see demand top pandemic levels
articles.content_orig:
During the Covid-19 pandemic, Greg Silverman watched an MTA bus driver pull over on Manhattan's Upper West Side, let his passengers off and run across the street toward him.
Silverman, who runs New York nonprofit West Side Campaign Against Hunger, initially thought the driver wanted to use the bathroom at the church where the food distribution was taking place. Instead, the man asked, "Can I get some food?"
"He was a full-time employee," Silverman said. "You are an essential personnel, making the city survive and you need food."
Now, Silverman said, his organization has seen demand surpass even the levels it observed during that time of crisis when the U.S. economy ground to a halt — and many of the people now seeking food also have jobs. Silverman expects the nonprofit to distribute as much as 6 million pounds of food this year.
"The height of the pandemic was not the height of need, by any means," he said.
The pressure on the emergency food system extends beyond New York. Nationally, use of charitable food programs remains elevated as sustained inflation makes it harder for Americans to afford food, housing and healthcare. Higher prices come at the same time that the federal government has restricted food aid.
The Department of Agriculture's latest annual report found that 13.7% of U.S. households, roughly 18.3 million households, experienced food insecurity in 2024. That rate was significantly higher than in every year from 2016 through 2021.
The pandemic initially brought a surge in demand for charitable food programs, which was followed by government support. In the years that followed, pandemic-era policies such as expanded Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, benefits, the enhanced child tax credit and school meal programs phased out as inflation spiked.
"This is not because you can't go to work," said City Harvest President Carlos Rodriguez. "Primarily, your work and your wages are just not keeping up with the way costs have gone up in the last five years alone."
City Harvest, which works with food providers across the five boroughs of New York, told CNBC 1 in 5 New Yorkers is currently experiencing food insecurity, or limited access to enough food because of a lack of money or other resources. That is up from 1 in 6 a year earlier, and 1 in 8 before the pandemic.
Average monthly visits to food pantries and soup kitchens in New York are also 85% higher than before the pandemic, said Rodriguez.
In the Federal Reserve's October Beige Book , the central bank's New York regional branch described a sharp rise in first-time food pantry users. One nonprofit leader told the Federal Reserve Bank of New York that the strain was comparable to the pandemic, "but without the same philanthropic and government support."
Data from Plentiful, a technology platform that connects people with food pantries and tracks their usage, also points to growing demand and limited resources.
"For pantries using our reservation and pre-registration features, we see that the overwhelming majority of those are at or over capacity," said Catherine Compitello, CEO of Plentiful. "Demand is growing while supply is not."
First-time users of Plentiful in New York City rose roughly 56% from August to October, Compitello said. It was the second-largest fall surge since 2016; the only larger one came during last year's federal government shutdown, when delayed SNAP benefits drove more people to seek food assistance.
Compitello said that when families have trouble affording essentials, they often prioritize healthcare, transportation, childcare and utilities, leaving food as the expense they cut back on.
Demand for food banks is rising in other regions of the country, and nonprofits are facing their own operational challenges as they try to meet it.
A spokesperson for the Los Angeles Regional Food Bank told CNBC the organization's diesel bill more than doubled in September, to roughly $75,000, adding to the cost of delivering food and running refrigerated trucks.
Demand in the region is also spiking. Distribution in the Los Angeles area for January through September totaled 116 million pounds of food and grocery products — the equivalent of 93 million meals — and slightly higher than a near-record year in 2025, according to the Los Angeles Regional Food Bank.
Federal food aid changes have exacerbated the problems. Rodriguez of City Harvest described SNAP as a first line of defense against hunger, saying the program can provide as many as nine meals for every one meal the organization provides. But City Harvest has estimated at least 8.7% of SNAP recipients in New York City lost benefits over the past year, after congressional Republicans and President Donald Trump approved work certification requirements and changes to eligibility.
The pressure is also mounting in Los Angeles County, where roughly 260,000 CalFresh recipients are subject to expanded federal work requirements that took effect in June. CalFresh is California's version of SNAP.
That does not mean all 260,000 will lose benefits, since people who meet the work requirements or qualify for an exemption can remain eligible. But a Los Angeles Regional Food Bank spokesperson told CNBC the changes add another layer of uncertainty for households already struggling with food costs.
In Atlanta, the pressure extends beyond the city itself to the surrounding region. The Atlanta Community Food Bank serves about 270,000 households a month, or nearly 700,000 people, through partner pantries across North Georgia. President and CEO Kyle Waide said the number of people it serves has jumped more than 70% in five years.
"Much of that increase is among people whose incomes are too high to qualify for federal benefit programs," said Waide.
Under current SNAP guidelines in Georgia, most households must have gross monthly income at or below 130% of the federal poverty level to qualify. They must also meet a separate net income test. For fiscal 2027, which began Oct. 1, the gross income limit is $2,960 a month for a household of three, or about $35,520 annually, and $3,575 a month for a household of four, or $42,900 a year.
More than 60% of Atlanta Community Food Bank clients have household incomes above the cutoff for SNAP eligibility, Waide said, generally in the mid-to-upper $30,000 range depending on household size. The food bank does not collect everyone's income, he said, but the figure is based on survey estimates.
Given those dynamics, Waide said he does not expect the need to ease.
"We're preparing for the level of demand to stay where it is today, or even increase more," Waide said. "We don't see a big source of relief coming anytime soon."

articles.title_orig: China sentences official to death for spying for foreign country
articles.title_zh: China sentences official to death for spying for foreign country
articles.content_orig:
China has sentenced a government official to death for handing over state secrets and classified documents to a foreign intelligence agent.
In a public post, Monday, China’s National Administration of State Secrets Protection said the convicted official was approached and recruited by a foreign woman while working overseas.
It is extremely rare for China to disclose that it has sentenced someone to death for espionage, or publish details on proceedings involving national security.
The post did not mention where the official was posted, but gave his surname as Ma, and said he had been approached by a woman named ‘Kailin,’ who initially said she was interested to learn Chinese. It did not say what the woman’s nationality was.
After their relationship developed, ‘Kailin’ began shifting their chats to “politically sensitive” topics and major international developments, and convinced Ma to hand over sensitive information about the personnel and operations of a Chinese institution in the country, according to prosecutors.
Kailin later introduced Ma to her other colleagues and told him that if he did not become an agent for their country, they would tip off the Chinese government about his activities. Ma then signed a pledge of loyalty, starting down the path “being consumed by darkness, and doomed beyond redemption,” the statement said.
The official later returned to China and sent “hundreds” of classified intelligence documents to the foreign agent in return for a fixed monthly income with additional bonus when he provided key material, according to the statement.
China’s prosecutor found Ma sent nine documents classified as state secrets and 26 documents classified as confidential in return for more than $150,000 for the espionage activities.
The state secrets administration’s post offered a stern warning to Chinese citizens to “maintain vigilance in our social and personal lives, adhere strictly to workplace discipline, and guard against being targeted, manipulated or exploited by hostile actors.”
The verdict comes as China steps up its anti-espionage efforts as its strategic rivalry with the US-led west deepens.
In 2023 China broadened the scope of its already sweeping counter-espionage law to expand the definition of espionage from covering state secrets and intelligence to any “documents, data, materials or items related to national security and interests,” without specifying specific parameters for how these terms are defined.
Earlier this year its spy agency warned that China’s young people were being duped by foreign forces into shirking hard work and prioritizing their individual emotions at the expense of national development.
The post from the State Security Ministry’s official account warned young people to stay vigilant against “complex opinion traps” and any “lying flat” narratives that propagate the message that hard work is futile.

articles.title_orig: Dive bar forces 18% tip onto customer’s bill — then hits them with snarky attitude
articles.title_zh: Dive bar forces 18% tip onto customer’s bill — then hits them with snarky attitude
articles.content_orig:
A dive bar in Atlanta is allegedly hitting patrons with a “mandatory” 18% gratuity fee — and customers are incensed.
Last week on Reddit , Georgia diners spotted a scathing review of The Local, a popular hangout in the Poncey-Highland neighborhood of Atlanta. “This is a dive bar with counter service,” wrote the disgruntled diner. “You order at a register and sit back down.”
The arbitrary charge at the unpretentious, no-frills neighborhood pub comes amid the ongoing outrage over out-of-control tipping culture . It’s a merciless movement that pressures consumers to pay an additional 10% to 25% (or more) almost everywhere — from everyday eateries to self-service kiosks.
But the hole-in-the-wall watering hole wasn’t a place where many of the Peach State’s patrons expected a mandatory tipping charge.
“They call your name when the food is ready and you go pick it up. What is this fee for?” the unhappy customer asked, to which The Local’s owner replied, “You’re free to go elsewhere.”
Representatives for The Local did not immediately respond to The Post’s request for a comment — though online, plenty of people claiming to be patrons of The Local did, triggering a wave of upset across social media.
While online whistleblowers are calling obligatory gratuity a “scam,” others are bashing “a–hole” managers for failing to properly pay their employees and exploiting customers.
“And elsewhere I will go! Mandatory fee for counter service?!? Ain’t no way!” wrote an irate Redditor.
“Nope, [it’s a] sh- -ty practice to lure people in with “lower” food prices [then] to slap the fees afterwards,” another agreed. “All prices should be set with everything already included.”
“They won’t be getting a dime from me or my family,” a separate anti-tipper spat.
“It’s like a death spiral,” chimed another, blasting bars and restaurants for passing the buck onto the public rather than pay staffers a decent living wage.
Virtual vitriol notwithstanding, the war on tipping rages on — with no clear end in sight.
A New Jersey mom recently castigated a local restaurant for sneaking an additional 18% gratuity charge onto her $300 bill after a gratuity had already been applied.
Michael Knowles, a political commentator, also took to the internet in anger after being asked to tip at an automated checkout station at the airport.
“Would I like to leave a tip?” Knowles growled in a buzzy Facebook bulletin, shaming corporate greed.
“I have not seen a single employee, I have scanned my own Perrier and now the robot wants me to tip it.”
